review_text_raw:
A supernatural horror story where you use a missing person's phone (texting contacts/viewing photos/reading e-mail/other apps or social media) to figure out what happened to them. Not the same but it gives a similar feel to me as a game like Orwell.

I don't really enjoy horror games in general so I preferred playing this game as a mystery. I didn't really care for the random 'horror' sound effects or imagery. I was a bit disappointed when the plot went for [spoiler]the sci-fi twist. It's alright but I would have liked a regular, more realistic thing. It felt like something outside of your control with no real foreshadowing or buildup. There is nothing to suggest that it was possible and even after you learn about it you can't go back and see much in a new light. It might be nice if they at least put something random about the dangers of AI or something.[/spoiler]

Aside from the general phone-searching there are some minigames. They aren't too tough but one might be harder if you're not a native english speaker. One minigame is taking a jumbled list of words and making the right sentence out of it. However, it's not enough to get an equivalent meaning- you have to get the word order exactly right. For example, 'Meet me and I'll show ya this weekend' is wrong but 'Meet me this weekend and I'll show ya' is right.

Worth a look if you're fine with learning about the missing person story through phone history and dialogue.

Other thoughts:[list]
[*] It's a little annoying that in order to get the 'good' ending you have to [spoiler]manipulate people because there's no way to convince them otherwise.[/spoiler]
[*] I would have liked multiple save slots.
[*] It's nice that it can be set to automatically skip text on repeat playthroughs.
[*] Pretty much no settings to adjust (only subtitles). I would've liked at least volume and resolution options.
[*] Some inconsistencies/strange things: [spoiler]She met Taylor on Spark but had been following him on Jabbr 3 months ago. Cassie's AMA from 3 months ago is still continuing even though it closed (you get to ask a question)? The article mentions a back-and-forth between genders but you're forced to repeat the female gender and use one of the three pre-selected photos (it seems like other pictures don't progress the story). Why is it assimilating the 'weak'? From what I understand it's somehow taking control of a person and building a world out of their simulacrum (online personification?)? And then discarding the physical body for some reason because they can only lure in one person on Spark before they're useless?[/spoiler]
[*] A bunch of grammar and spelling errors and incorrect subtitles.
[*] Only crashed randomly once.
[/list]

review_text_raw:
[h1][b] TLDR: While not noteworthy in any direction, it’s a decent low-budget mystery/thriller that is acceptable for its price. [/b] [/h1]

[h1]PROS: [/h1]
➕Good concept with phone imitation and believable features
➕Multiple decision-based endings


[h1]CONS: [/h1]
➖Severe lack of options, not even fullscreen toggle or audio options??
➖Missing some essential phone features, like ease of scrolling through tons of text messages or jumping to specific times in videos
➖Some cringe voice acting/FMV

[h1] [b] Content (Game world/Narrative) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The game world takes place entirely on a phone, using the phone's UI screen. It’s a very simple imitation, but most of it works as you’d expect a phone to function. You have various apps that you go through, including email, messaging, Twitter-like  social media, photos, and dating apps. As far as a phone imitation goes, I’d say the world is fairly good, though it is missing some obvious features like being able to click on a point-in-time on a video to move to that section, or scrolling through hundreds of text messages. Otherwise, it’s good. 

The narrative focuses on a girl named Anna, who has seemingly disappeared. For some reason, Anna’s phone ends up in your possession and you have to sleuth around to figure out what happened and how to find her. 
The story has branching paths that ultimately comes down to which person you end up believing and siding with, as well as specific choices along the way that influence the ending of the game. 
I got the “Worst” ending, but was still satisfied with my playthrough because I did everything sensible and logical that I would do. To achieve the better endings, you have to do questionably moral things like [spoiler]siding with a sex offender when you have limited information[/spoiler], or [spoiler]confessing love to Anna’s best friend while pretending to be Anna.[/spoiler] In a way, it's sleazy and morally ambiguous, but I do also understand the phishing aspect of it and needing to obtain information any way possible. 
In the end, I found the story to be only “Ok” . The antagonist of a [spoiler]rogue AI[/spoiler] wasn’t very exciting or scary at the end. 

[h1][b] Gameplay (Mechanics/Difficulty) – [6/10] [/b] [/h1]
The general gameplay loop is to explore around the phone UI solving puzzles to advance the plot. 
The mechanics remind me of a watered-down version of The Rootrees Are Dead (great game, check out my review [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/Synikx/recommended/2754380?snr=1_5_9__402]here[/url]), how you have to use hints to sleuth around a phone for information. I’d say about 70% of the puzzles in the game consist of either decoding messages or pictures, whereas the other 30% is about researching information. 
The picture/message decoding consists of either aligning pictures correctly, or putting text messages in the correct order. I found the picture puzzles to be much more challenging. The researching of information is where it’s similar to Rootrees where you need to look through emails or messages to find correct information for things like passwords. 
While the mechanics were fine, I would have much preferred the quantity of research to picture/text decoding to be reversed, that is 70% research and 30% decode. I felt like the decoding was a bit out of place. 

The difficulty is generally easy. I was stumped a few times, but the game allows a skip or nudges you in the right direction after a little bit. The only challenging part is figuring out the very specific choices to get the better endings. 

[h1] [b] Technical (Graphics/Performance) – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Graphics were okay. Most of the game is a phone UI, with the remaining parts being FMV or pictures. I felt that the UI looks simple, but believable. The FMV and pictures were high quality and numerous, especially in public settings, so I appreciated the realistic approach. I’d say this is around PS4-era graphics. 
Performance was flawless, zero issues. 
I do want to call out the atrocious graphical settings. I don’t think I’ve ever seen a game with less options. I think the only two are language and subtitles. Not even audio volume or full screen or resolution. 
I didn’t notice any bugs. 

1440p @ 240hz | installed on SSD  

[h1] [b] Audio – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
There wasn’t much, if any music. 
There is ample voice acting, and half of it was super cringe. Anna did a decent job. Greg was just terrible. Taylor has ups and downs. Ashley is decent as well. 

[h1] [b] Replay Factor (Longevity) – [4/10] [/b] [/h1]
Decent replay value due to the multiple endings, but you probably need a guide for the route on how to get there. Otherwise, just achievements and easter eggs. 

[h1] [b] Final Verdict – [5/10] [/b] [/h1]
Simulacra is a horror game that takes place entirely on a phone screen, with you being the user operating the phone. This isn’t an overly terrifying game, though there is a few jump scares, and I found the plot to be okay, which is generally the linchpin with these more “Visual novel”-type games with less gameplay depth, so all things considered, it’s a fairly good game, especially for the price. 

I don’t have too many big issues with the game, just smaller ones. 
The graphical options are terrible, but thankfully, I was able to use alt+enter to play in windowed mode, since there’s no borderless option. 
I’d have liked better phone functionality, namely being able to click to any point in time for videos and ease of scrolling through dozens of text messages. Everyone has been using smartphones for decades at this point, so these basic features should be available. 
Lastly, the voice acting was pretty cringy. Cringe was generally the norm, with average performances being the exception. 

Otherwise, the gameplay through small puzzles and sleuthing, and the story, while not exceptional, were both enough to keep me interested until I hit the credits. 
There’s a lot of things that could be improved, but for the price, I think it’s a solid game worth checking out. 

[h1] [b] Recommend? (Price) [Y/N] [/b] [/h1]
[h1]Yes[/h1]
$5 is an acceptable price considering it takes around ~4 hours to beat for a single playthrough and offers multiple endings. Sale price of $1 is very good. 

You can find my curator page here: https://steamcommunity.com/groups/Synik_GR

review_text_raw:
[h1]Short but Intuitive Mystery Game[/h1]

[i]SIMULACRA[/i] is a modern FMV game that features great sleuthing gameplay with some minor horror elements. After I 100% the entire game, I can safely say this is one of the better indie visual novel titles I've encountered if not for the gameplay alone. I will try to keep this review mostly spoiler-free, but as usual with my reviews for narrative-based games, I will have spoilers for stuff I feel the need to comment on. 

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[olist]
[*] The gameplay and puzzles are fun yet intuitive. I like the process of fixing corrupted messages and images to not only progress the game but to also discover more about the characters.
[*] Lots of "show don't tell" moments that exemplify how the developers understand that this is a visual medium and that it is important to use the visuals to their advantage. For example, though it's never stated Anna is into fitness, one of the first image puzzles is of her posing with weights to give the idea that she is an active person. This is great  yet subtle storytelling I love to see in these types of games. 
[*] The text messages and dating profiles are pretty genuine. There are definitely people out there who act exactly like the ones in this game.
[*] The narrative does a lot to try and make you question the motives of the characters and their backgrounds in a meaningful way so that the suspense is maintained the entire playthrough. 
[*] [spoiler] The main antagonist being a serial killer HAL-9000-esque AI in the phone itself is fascinating in its own right, and the fact that its goal is to create perfect versions of otherwise "pathetic worms" as it refers to people it deems as as such, is great social commentary on how people are obsessed with their public image online to the point that they are no longer genuinely themselves. The antagonist also serves as a personification of tech companies and their obsession to mold people into their idealized image through deceptive practices and establishing trust by packaging things in digestible ways. For example, during the phone reset, the soothing sounds and use of cool hues is meant to contrast with the otherwise invasive questions and disturbing content the OS system tries to get you to answer in detail. In the end, you get the best ending by impressing the AI with your ability to manipulate the characters--an interesting moral dilemma to say the least!  [/spoiler]
[*] The menus and apps look and feel like their real version counterparts. Very good overall graphical presentation. 
[*] Small and subtle changes to show you are progressing through the story. For example, [spoiler] Anna's picture in the home screen will change expression the closer you get to the ending of the game. [/spoiler]
[*] Lots of small things to discover just by exploring the phone (which you can get achievements for). 
[*] Sped up dialog loading for additional playthroughs is a great QoL feature. 
[/olist]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[olist]
[*] The voice acting and FMV sequences come across as cheesy most of the time, if not overacted. 
[*] The autosave feature means you can't go back to a previous part like you can with most visual novels. This means that if you messed up on a certain decision, you may have to restart the entire run just to redo it. This can be pretty frustrating. 
[*] No option to skip puzzles for additional playthroughs means you'll have to do them over and over again which can be pretty tedious if you're trying to get all the achievements. 
[*] The dialogue choices you  need to appease and have Taylor trust you come across as a bit too flirty at times.
[*] Greg and Ashley come across as too angry and distrustful to the player character depending on certain choices made. Meanwhile, Taylor comes across as too trusting. This is why sometimes it's not very good to have a faceless protagonist--we don't really understand what the characters see in [i]you[/i] when the interactions are so minimal. 
[*] The horror elements are too on the nose with the jumpscares. Though the phone OS does have some good subtle horror elements, more of this throughout the game would have been way better overall. 
[*] [spoiler] Though I like the idea of the antagonist, having it type in predictable shaky font and using distorted visuals is pretty cliche. Personally, I think it'd come across scarier if it were way more subtle like how it is when the phone resets.[/spoiler]
[/olist]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Worth at least one playthrough--though playing it blind is your best bet. The gameplay alone makes it worth it. For additional playthroughs, some patience is required. Watch additional endings via recordings if that's not your thing.

review_text_raw:
When you are a mature person and your childhood and carefree days are already over, you have kinda stressful job, you don't feel like playing hard games, or games where you have to concentrate a lot. Sometimes, you just want to come over to your place. make yourself a cup of tea and just relax on comfortable chair and just enjoy some kinda easy game. Preferably, with a mouse only controls.

But to be honest, you need to be ready that games will be strange, or better call them weird or maybe even creepy in some kinda way, cause variety of the titles, that can be played with mouse only is pretty limited and you should expect only chinese visual novels, or some nonsense clickers, or easy tower defense games, or some puzzle logic games.

Or it can be a game like Simulacra. I am not even sure how to call this genre, but what I really do know for sure - this game is completely stupid :) But, in a good funny way. They call it a simulation game, which is kinda fair, but doesn't cover the whole idea of this game. 

So, you start the game playing as not a man, not a woman, just whoever the hell you are, sex is not specified in this game. You found a smartphone and this is where the whole stupid part is about to start. I mean like, imagine you are that person who found a phone, okay? What you gonna do? For me it's completely obvious and easy - if phone is unlockable, you simply need to find someone with a name Mom, Dad, Sister, Boyfriend, Dog in a contact list, call one of them and let them know that you found this device and return it as soon as possible. In case phone is locked, you just need to go to the police station and give it to them for the further actions. Easy as that, don't you think so? But not for our protagonist! Instead all of this, he/she decides to play around with this phone and read messages/mail, check web history, tinder-alike app - I mean like literally everything what you don't have to do, when you find someone's phone, cause this is simply embarassing. For the whole game I had that feeling that I was playing as a retard, who had no job, no personal life, no entertainment sources, literally nothing, so that phone was a greatest relief ever. 

But, on the other hand, if that person wouldn't be that miserable and pathetic and wouldn't check that messages and videos on the camera roll - he wouldn't realize that phones belonged to someone who was desperately crying for help, stucked in some kinda danger. The more you click on that stupid phone the more stranger and uglier everything becomes, and you have to solve some kinda puzzles. All these puzzle things are more like "choose the right answer" in dialogues with a random people, talking about phone's owner, which is also a random person for you lol, which you shouldn't care about at all and all these combinations of answers lead you to different endings. Plus you have to recreate some corrupted messages, by putting words in the right order and renew corrupted photos by clicking on image pieces at the right order. Time to time, you will see ugly screamers on the phone, whose aim is to scarry you and like, to be honest, this one of the most ridiculous things in this game, cause I was laughing all the time when that was appearing on the screen, so I can't say that this game is a horror experience, it's more "wannabe horror game" , trying to be mysterious and creepy all the way ends up with a pretty shallow and a bit boring idea.

However, I can recommend this game. It brings you some fresh new experience and can be funny a little bit plus you can relax after a busy stressful day by just clicking on the dialogue options and solving pretty easy puzzles trying to figure out what the hell is going on there. 

So, to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you: 

+ Feel like playing some easy game, where is no need for high concentration
+ Are a Black Mirror TV show fan and like all this paranoic idea about how it can be bad somewhere in the future for us with all these high-tech devices
+ Don't agree with me, that carrying a phone to the police station would be the best idea in this situation :)
+ Just looking for a new experience

Avoid this game if you:

- Don't like illogical games, with a stupid protagonist who has no idea what the hell is he doing 
- Have no desire to try something new and unusual

Enjoy!

But, on the other hand, if that person wouldn't be that miserable and pathetic and wouldn't check that messages and videos on the camera roll - he wouldn't realize that phones belonged to someone who was desperately crying for help, stucked in some kinda danger. The more you click on that stupid phone the more stranger and uglier everything becomes, and you have to solve some kinda puzzles. All these puzzle things are more like "choose the right answer" in dialogues with a random people, talking about phone's owner, which is also a random person for you lol, which you shouldn't care about at all and all these combinations of answers lead you to different endings. Plus you have to recreate some corrupted messages, by putting words in the right order and renew corrupted photos by clicking on image pieces at the right order. Time to time, you will see ugly screamers on the phone, whose aim is to scarry you and like, to be honest, this one of the most ridiculous things in this game, cause I was laughing all the time when that was appearing on the screen, so I can't say that this game is a horror experience, it's more "wannabe horror game" , trying to be mysterious and creepy all the way ends up with a pretty shallow and a bit boring idea. However, I can recommend this game. It brings you some fresh new experience and can be funny a little bit plus you can relax after a busy stressful day by just clicking on the dialogue options and solving pretty easy puzzles trying to figure out what the hell is going on there. Sad to say that I had to refund this. The premise seemed solid based on the store page - trying to piece together clues to someone's disappearance when you only have their phone - and the general interface was well done, but that was about it. My first hour of playing this mostly consisted of:

[list]
[*] Listening to overdramatic, very slowly worded voice messages.
[*] Piecing together "corrupted" pictures and texts that had absolutely nothing to do with Anna's disappearance. 
[*] Wondering if a proofreader was ever used for this game. Most of the articles and texts gave me the impression that English isn't the developer's first language. While I have nothing against that, coming across awkward grammar really took the immersion out of a mostly text-based game.
[*] Sitting through consecutive rounds of text-vomit finger-pointing from Greg and Taylor. I truly detest people who text at a rate of 50 messages/min when a single sentence would have sufficed. I didn't think it could get any worse, but in came the relationship drama...
[*] An overall disconnect between the gameplay and the plot. A girl disappears with clear hints of some non-human entity behind it, so why am I wasting my time investigating the sorry backgrounds of two garden-variety losers?
[/list]

Maybe the game gets better beyond the 1.7-hour point, but I really didn't have the patience to sit through constant notifications from the Male MC Idiot Express while waiting for some actual horror story to happen. Honestly, I'd have been happier to just shut the damn phone off and actually set out to find Anna door to door. At least then the "investigation" would have felt more productive.

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is a found phone horror game. The premise of the game is that you (the unknown, nameless protagonist – but presumably *you*, the actual player) found a phone out on your front porch that belongs to a woman named Anna. There’s something off about the phone, though; it keeps glitching out, a number of the files on it are messed up, there’s some creepypasta-esque flashes of the screen changing to horrifying images – and of course it quickly becomes evident from the frantic messages you get from her boyfriend that Anna has gone missing.

The game’s basic premise is exploring Anna’s phone. You decrypt some images and text messages via very simple minigames, but most of it is a choices-matter narrative, as you interact with not only Anna’s boyfriend, but a funny guy named Taylor on Spark (a dating/hookup app that *totally* isn’t Tinder) who had been flirting with Anna, as well as messages from Ashley, Anna’s best friend. You browse a few in-game websites, make a few phone calls from phone numbers you find on them and hidden in various images, and gradually unravel the mystery of what happened to Anna over the course of the game.

This is something of a hybrid of a simple puzzle game and Telltale’s sort of narrative storytelling, where you have a list of dialogue choices and they influence how other characters react to you. There is actually a branching narrative – the choices you make actually influence which endings you can access as you try to save Anna, only to discover that things aren’t so easy, and how you treat the characters affects how they interact with you. If you’re a jerk to someone, they won’t trust you and will be a jerk back; if you’re nice to them, they’ll be more trusting. But at the same time, you can lie about who you are to various people in the game, and while sometimes they’ll figure it out, other times you’ll slot right in as a trusted person and be able to get what you need out of them.

Indeed, pretense is a major theme of the game – people aren’t quite who they present themselves to be online, and the fronts they put up often don’t match who they are (or, indeed, who they perceive themselves to be). Is Anna’s boyfriend really still together with her, or did they break up, and is he stalking her? There’s a bunch of sexual predators on Spark – is Taylor one of them? Does Ashley have ulterior motives in her friendship with Anna?

I’d like to say that the biggest flaw with this game is that the resolution is, perhaps, a bit on the nose. While I approve of this new age of horror, and coming up with a new spooky villain, I also didn’t feel like it did a good enough job of reinforcing the manipulation angle of social media, instead simply resorting to outright mind control, which was a lost opportunity.

However, I think the actual largest flaw with this game is that it is just okay. It is a clever idea, and there are some fun conceits in there, but I have to say at the end I was left feeling just lukewarm about it. When I play a game, or finish a game, I want a sense of satisfaction. But this was just sort of an experience I had. It wasn’t bad, but it wasn’t particularly excellent, either.

If you’ve never played a game like this before, and somehow got this for free or as part of a bundle, it’d be worth a spin to just try out something new. But at the same time, I’m left feeling like it’s hard to recommend that someone go out of their way to experience it, and when I recommend something, I want to actually be able to say to someone “Yes, you should go play this game.”

I wasn’t left with that feeling here, as while it is overall decent, it is all just a little bit flat, and the jump scares don’t manage to really carry the horror of the game very well.

!!!!! THIS REVIEW WILL *NOT* CONTAIN ANY STORY SPOILERS !!!!!

Simulacra is a short single-player experience that takes notes heavily from games such as "Her Story", "Emily is Away", and is eerily similar to "Sara is Missing". Having only played Simulacra, and not having played the others, I wouldn't feel right calling it merely a clone, and so I'll let it stand on its own.

Stemming originally from the point-and-click Adventure Game genres, these new detective-style games seem to be a welcome twist on an old idea. In Simulacra, you play, essentially, yourself. A strange phone has been left on your doorstep, and with seemingly nothing else to do for the day, you find yourself drawn into a mystery that only get stranger as more clues are discovered. 

The masterful design places you in control of the aforementioned phone, and in turn, of eight different phone apps, each more revealing than the last. The apps, meant to mimic modern day social media apps, are your wealth of information, and it shows (as I'm sure the creator intended) exactly how easy it can be to find someone using only a handful of these apps. As the story unravels, it becomes clear that something isn't quite right, and not everyone may be telling the truth. This game was packaged in with a Humble Bundle I purchased, and I was delighted with the experience, which I will outline below.

For a story told through different apps, I found that it (the story) never lost its pacing. As you hope with all good mysteries, I was completely enthralled, and intent on finding out exactly what happened. The lack of soundtrack is made up for with the addition of a host of spooky and scary sounds, ranging from low knocks on a nearby door, to terrifying schreeches from unlocked videos and glitches. This brings me to one of my gripes with the game: the minigame puzzles. 

While the minigames are a welcome break from the plethora of text in the game, I found their solutions to often be sort of convoluted. In fact, the only times that I felt unimmersed were the times I sat, hands on my head, attempting to solve a glorified word jumble, only to find that the answer was often unclear. Similarly, I had a difficult time figuring out the photograph puzzles, in which you stack and unstack layers of corrupted files until you find the ideal stacking formation that removes all corruption. Thankfully, these minigames were few and far in between, and most of my time was spent enjoying the different situations and obstacles in the way of my investigation. Hopping between apps in the game is as effortless as it is in real life, and made for very smooth transitions, and very little downtime as I progressed. 

The characters are pretty solid. It's a rich cast, and I was thankful to hear a notable quality in the performance of the actors. While there were one or two lines which made me cringe, the overall performances were fantastic, which bodes well for any completionists who plan to play multiple runs of this game, in order to live all the different outcomes. The voice acting was mostly really solid, and the video performances followed suit. I honestly could have done without all the spooky whispers and door knocks that were staggered throughout the playthrough. I understand their intention was to heighten the atmosphere of fear, but with the quality of the storytelling, I'm not sure that any additional atmosphere was really needed. Instead of shocking me, the rare jump scare attempts and 'spooky imagery' instead removed me from the story, and reminded me that I was, in fact, completely safe in my computer chair, instead of inside a strange house looming over a stranger's phone. Like the minigames, though, the attempted jump scares are sparsely placed within the game, and didn't detract from my overall enjoyment.

The total of my playtime consists of a single playthrough of the game, so use that as a measuring stick for how long a standard run will last. Despite enjoying the game very much, I do not think I'll replay it, mostly because I don't have a completionist mentality, and I was very satisfied from a single playthrough, but I definitely intend to do some research on what my decisions could have changed. If you're in the mood for a quick, but good story with compelling characters and a great design, than I'd highly recommend Simulacra. 

Thanks to the development team! You can tell a lot of love went into this game, and it was so much fun to play!

A lost phone appears in your grasp out of nowhere. When you peaked inside, you discovered a creepy video of someone else either asking for assistance or not. In this game, you are abruptly connected to unusual occurrences that put the people nearby in possibly deadly situations.


[H1] Visual: [/H1]
The UX and UI of this game are quite straightforward but interesting in their aesthetic design. Every "app" in this game has been designed in such a way that it is simple to grasp what it is and what kind of hint it is intended to give the player. A genuine smartphone design is featured in the game, along with a number of in-game applications modeled after well-known mobile applications including social media, apps, emails and other type of apps.

[H1] Audio [/H1]
Simulacra's original soundtrack will play during the main menu; it isn't very remarkable, but it wonderfully complements the game. The audio in this game is quite loud and intentionally intended to jump scare the player during the game's horror scenes. The voice acting of the actors aren't really good either. There is nothing else really interesting other than that.


[H1] Gameplay: [/H1]

Simulacra provides a decent horror experience. In this game, the choices you made along the way are tightly linked to one another. This game includes a memo so that you won't get lost if you forgot about the tasks you "need" to do. However, aside from the primary objective—which is to find Anna—they are not really a must-do. It is sometimes necessary to stop doing what you "should" do (based on memo) in order to achieve a different result (that would suit the player better). These messages may appear insignificant, but they contain information that the player will need later on. The difference in outcome will not be visible right away because they are sometimes piling on top of one another before reaching the turning point. The player would also need to uncover puzzles and collectibles throughout the game. In this game, finding those kinds of items is necessary in order to progress the story, unlike other games where they are optional. The puzzles are straightforward to solve; they consist of jumbled words, and all you need to do is choose the appropriate text to complete it. 


[spoiler] If you want to complete the game to the fullest extent possible, you will need to play it more than once because various accomplishments can be unlocked separately and you can only choose one of them. As the game has a few but game-breaking bugs, it would be more practical and less risky to just concentrate on one path at a time rather than reloading a backup save just to get all the achievements in a single run. Although it is possible to do it with the game saves and try to squeeze everything up in one playthrough. I suggest making backup files after chatting with Ashley about "who's at fault."

[/spoiler]


[H1] Controls [/H1]

Keyboard and Mouse are the only way to play it.

[H1] Pricing [/H1]

Worth the price

Simulacra is an interactive horror movie displayed through an emulated mobile phone screen.  You've got someone else's phone and for some reason you're texting her boyfriend and watching spooky videos because something went wrong.  Spooky technology glitches! oooOOOoooo. 

I think FMV can be an excellent tool in storytelling and video game creation if used right.  Looking at games that worked, like Press X Not To Die and Mortal Kombat, you can see why.  Simulacra isn't one of the ones that works.  The story is below Blair Witch 4 kind of stuff, it's not gripping.  The bits where you're texting other people is badly written.  I understand the developers wanted to emulate a mobile phone, but looking at my 4K monitor being wasted displaying a 9:16 aspect ratio is just depressing.

There's better ways to tell a story than we can see in Simulacra.  For less money than they're asking for this you could rent any schlock horror film online and have a far better time, with better writing and acting, too.  If you did end up with this in the Humble Bundle and accidentally launched it, be aware the game crashes when you try to exit, and you have to go find the rogue process and kill it.

TL;DR: Posting this review to help Steam out, since this game does NOT deserve such praise. Honestly, I would have been annoyed but said screw it if it was at "Very Positive"... but overwhelmingly positive? It literally does nothing new, innovative, or even good. In fact, I'd say the only thing it accomplished was copying things done many times before it in an absolutely terrible way. It was a slog to get through from beginning to end. I can honestly say it combined all the crappiest parts of horror movie trailers, the worst creepypastas and a s****y jigsaw puzzle together in a terrible phone-shaped package that lasted for WAY too long. It was 30 minutes of terrible content somehow stretched into 3 hours. In other words, if you get it in a bundle like me, go ahead and stop playing when you decide the moment is right. It's not going to get better.

Got this from the "Overwhelmingly Positive" Humble Bundle. How in the actual f*** is this game "Overwhelmingly Positive" ????? Kids review bomb awesome games on here all the time, and this managed to survive that for so long? I'm legitimately confused and concerned. Did this game get massive press in some media targeted specifically towards children, and somehow avoid literally everyone else? Did the people who hate it just not care enough to leave a review? Again, were on Steam, so how?????

On a particularly boring night, I played the entire damn thing. The first 5 minutes in I already knew it was going to be terrible, but stupidly I played on, hoping for something redeeming to happen to justify the positive reviews and my time wasted. That obviously didn't happen.

Bad writing, bad puzzles, atrocious "scares" (literally all jumps, flashing images and noises, and even then not a single f***ing one even managed a startled shutter from me, with volume annoyingly high), all set to an all-too-overplayed by now "hey, play this game on this device/OS/form of communication" gimmick that I'm frankly by now beyond tired of game developers using as a replacement for an interesting story/plot/writing (Stories Untold is the most recent game to do it RIGHT AFAIK). It was cool like the first 100 times maybe, but I'm over it.

I also want to point out, I don't think I have EVER seen good writing/plot in a game that has characters communicating through a messaging system, then has every character using terrible grammar, punctuation, etc. It bugs the hell out of me.
1.It's usually inconsistent. Some chatacters just spring in and out of it randomly.
2.We're not all 12. Some people actually care about that kind of stuff, so it doesn't make sense to have EVERYONE at some point talking like the slow, overly emotional kid in class.
3.It isn't 1995 anymore. It's one thing to have every character talk like that when they're using AOL Instant Messenger, but for chrissakes, you actually have to make an EFFORT to screw up grammar the way these characters do on a modern cellphone with autocorrect. Ugh.

Simulacra, developed by Kaigan Games OÜ and published by Kaigan Games OÜ alongside Neon Doctrine, is a gripping and unnerving found-phone horror game that masterfully blends storytelling, mystery, and interactive gameplay. The game places players in the shoes of a person who discovers a lost phone belonging to a woman named Anna, who has mysteriously disappeared. What begins as a seemingly straightforward search quickly evolves into a dark, psychological thriller that unravels through the phone’s contents, offering an immersive narrative experience driven entirely by player interaction with texts, apps, videos, and social media. This innovative format taps into contemporary fears about technology and privacy, creating a tense and intimate atmosphere that keeps players hooked from start to finish.

At its core, Simulacra excels at storytelling through environmental and digital clues, requiring players to carefully sift through Anna’s phone for evidence to understand what happened to her. The game’s interface convincingly mimics a real smartphone, complete with calls, messages, emails, and even a creepy AI assistant named "Maya" that adds an additional layer of eerie presence. Players must navigate conversations, unlock apps, and decrypt files, which gradually reveal Anna’s troubled life and the sinister forces at play. The game’s narrative pacing is well-calibrated, steadily building suspense while offering occasional moments of emotional vulnerability that make Anna’s plight feel deeply personal and urgent.

Visually, Simulacra embraces a minimalistic but effective approach, using the phone’s screen as the main canvas for its storytelling. The user interface is polished and intuitive, making it easy to become engrossed in the investigation without distractions. The game’s use of sound design is particularly noteworthy — ambient noises, notification sounds, and voice messages all contribute to the growing sense of dread. The lack of traditional cinematic cutscenes is replaced by clever interactive sequences that heighten immersion and player agency, ensuring that every discovery feels earned and impactful.

One of the standout features of Simulacra is its branching narrative and multiple endings, which encourage players to explore different paths and decisions throughout the game. This replayability factor enhances the game’s value and allows for varied emotional outcomes, depending on the player’s choices. The writing is generally sharp, weaving together elements of horror, thriller, and drama while avoiding common genre clichés. The characters, though primarily seen through their digital personas, are well fleshed out, and the voice acting adds authenticity to the conversations, heightening the emotional stakes.

That said, Simulacra is not without its limitations. Some players might find the pacing slow during certain investigative segments, and the reliance on reading through extensive text may not appeal to everyone, especially those looking for more action-oriented gameplay. Additionally, the horror elements are more psychological and subtle rather than jump-scare-heavy, which might not satisfy fans expecting traditional scares. Technical issues, such as occasional app glitches or interface bugs, have also been reported but generally do not detract significantly from the overall experience.

Overall, Simulacra stands out as a unique and compelling title that pushes the boundaries of interactive horror by situating its narrative within the intimate space of a smartphone. Its creative storytelling approach, immersive sound design, and chilling atmosphere combine to deliver an experience that feels both modern and unsettling. For players who appreciate mystery, psychological horror, and narrative-driven games that challenge them to piece together a story from fragmented clues, Simulacra offers a memorable journey into the dark side of digital life and human vulnerability.

Rating: 9/10

Quite engaging visual novel using already seen by many setting of text quests. For me this kind of gameplay is not as shallow as it seems and does provide somewhat new experience, although I did have an experience of playing text quests or even writing them by myself way back then.

The atmosphere of typical detective storyline intersecting with personal relationships of a missing person the role of which we are playing in the process of dealing with all those unreal mystic-like happenings adds up a lot with its base gameplay.

Of course it’s not just a novel, but a horror too. And these specific elements don’t exactly work all of the time, though there are a few good examples, but mostly I got scared by sudden calls from a cop during my leisure-time reading of backed up messages. When talking about good examples, breaking the 4th wall is one of them - when you getting the choice of what’d you prefer, ‘A flying head or a headless body behind you’, I got little chills down my spine because regardless of what you chose, the following would sound like ‘Your hair smells nice’ or ‘Can I touch your hair?’, which, combined with the general atmosphere, is quite creepy and gets you tense a little (especially if there’s a whole ass room behind you).

Otherwise it’s somewhat exciting to play through this game simply because its main idea works very well and keeps you interested, though I won’t tell you an exact reasoning for this - play it yourself to get the hang of it.

Nevertheless, I’d like to add on to my positive thoughts a bit of dark sides.
Despite having a bunch of answer options during every possible dialogue, their consequences consist of several plot peculiarities:

1) Whether you get Taylor's trust or not

2) Will Ashley find out that her friend is missing

Well, that’s all. As you can see, there's not much variety here. Only these two options would subsequently affect the outcome you get - more precisely speaking, ending. You either lose everyone because you didn’t meet the requirements or save everyone instead because you dealt with it otherwise.

That’s quite shallow so to speak. It’s not a kinetic novel as most of them tend to struggle with, too straightforward and not to hard to understand either.
Considering the concept which this title has, I get a strong feeling that there could’ve been much more endings than we have as a result.

Also, referring to achievements, I’d like to blabber a bit more about it too.
Recalling that there’s not much variety here, going through your second playthrough for a ordinary click-clack to get a few achievement is an unbearable struggle that only messes up your perception of the game. Simulacra does not even allow you to watch videos simultaneously because of its ugly fullscreen resolution that you cannot change during the game.

As a conclusion, I did like it plot-wise, and maybe sometime later would consider playing its sequel. But when it comes to achievements, it’s not worth it - they are ruining your first impressions and forcing you to acquaint with its low-variety gameplay. Yeah, you can talk to people on Tinder, deal with other people struggles, sure, but it does not affect your main storyline and is present here only to give you achievements.

I’d say it’s good enough, but don’t ever hunt for achievements here.

Simulacra is a game about something. I'm not really sure what, since the game is practically foreshadowing its own inability to deliver on its buildup in many places, and the solution to the mystery had me wondering why there even was a mystery to solve, being that it was something which had little to do with anything that exists in the real world (though there is doubtless some deep philosophical meaning behind the Ghost of Facebook Profiles Past throwing someone off a building for not having enough followers on MySpace).
The story is told through a cast of characters, inlcuding, but not limited to: A man who you can convince to commit corporate espionage and B&E in one sentence each, a sex offender who couldn't shut up to save his life, and the girl who went missing, has her entire character arc revealed in chapter one and never gets any more developement aside from us finding out that everything she did was, in fact, understandable, if rude. All of these reserved seats on the short bus are caught up in a missing person case, but have to do it through the player character, who has his own character, and who can't count to his own IQ. The story is told through tweedle dee and tweedle dum figuring out ways to get more evidence, and the protagonist actually doing it.
The dialogue system is both good and bad. It's bad because the dialogue was bootlegged from Fallout 4, and rarely had the thing I wanted to say, and good in that they actaully manage to do more with it than Bethesda ever did. As stated, the two stooges figure out new ways to attack the case and figure things out, and you actaully do it with puzzling that ranges from "good" to "really bad". There are puzzles where you put together images such that htere's no corruption, which I liked,  puzzles where you unscramble sentences, which were rarely necessary but also rarely obnoxious, and there were puzzles where you have an article to draw information from, but the information in the article is more wrong than the information Bill Cosby the 2nd pulls out of thin air.
Don't worry about the horror elements, it's just a few loud noises and distorted images. So we have a game where the horror is token, the story is confusing, and the characters are dumb and/or pricks. It's technically perfectly adequate, but so are virtually all visual novels, and what extra this does amounts to set decoration. 3/10, since someone who is willing to not think too hard might find it artistically brilliant.

A rather short game about a missing person.

You work on the missing persons mobile phone throughout the game and interact with Apps and send messages to persons.
While doing so, through music and ambient sounds, and a scare from time to time, this game creates an extremely intense atmosphere and pulls you into it's world!

Very, very good game. Highly recommend playing it. The 4€ are not much to pay for a couple hours of enjoyment!

I played it for a bit more than 5h now in one day.
In this time I completed my first and therefore truthful to my character playthrough, with a rather satisfying, though not "good" ending.
This took me around 4-4.5h

The remaining time, and time that will add from now on, is used for achivements, since this game let's you have them rather easily by reaching certain optional objectives that are never stated anywhere though ;)
So if you like to get into some secret hunting: This might be a game for you!

At the time of writing this review, I completed 4 out of 5 endings.
All of which are different enought to have their own twist to them! Really nice.

I know what the last ending will result in, but the details are yet unknown.

There are some negative points though, as no game is perfect.

Since we are talking about a "mobile game port" (to my knowledge that is), there are some essentials lacking.

This game features no settings menu of any kind.
It is not possible to lower the audio, except through the OS' sound mixer ...
That is not acceptable, far less in a post TB (TotalBiscuit) world.
Being able to lower Sound, Music and/or Video (which is sparsely used), would make this a more proper PC-game.
Also I haven't seen the possibility to change resolution, though the game is played only on about 10% of the screen anyway (due to the type of game it is ...)

There are subtitles hidden in the help-menu in main menu.

Especially in the later part of the game, the music is a tad too loud in comparison with the voices, so understanding suffers from it.

Other than the just stated? Not much to complain about.

If you have ever wondered how ugly it could get in the event that AI were to take over, well, this game depicts one possible reality. 

Enjoyed it overall, but aiming to reach 100% completion left me with mixed feelings.


Simulacra is a modern take on a philosophical idea that originated in an essay called "Simulacra and Simulation" from 1981. It's simple, and yet, if you manage to reach any ending, and the true ending especially, you will likely ask yourself questions about how you approach your existence in our digitalised world.

The game has its flaws, but if you're okay with this format, then you will probably have a good time.


When I played Simulacra for the first time in 2018, I played it, and I enjoyed it a lot. I was impressed by the simplistic yet effective nature of the storytelling that was made relevant due to the then technologically transitional period: everyone learning how to use smartphones for almost anything. I also appreciated how little the game requires of you, safe for the patience to read, comprehend, observe, and stop to think for a moment, making it an easy recommendation for playing after a mentally and physically demanding day.

That was then. But what about now...?


Lately, I had been thinking a lot about the topics of Simulacra, Simulation, Simulacrum, and AI, so I decided to replay the game and complete it because I liked it so much my first time. It took me 2 playthroughs to reach completion. The first one took 4-5 hours, and the second - no more than 2-3. My recommendation if you were to seek completion within the day would be to do it with a guide next to you. Some achievements, especially the hidden one and the true ending, require noticing and doing a number of things, which could take you hours to nail by going back again and again -- which could be enjoyable if you're into that and are okay with spending more time with the game.

And here is a thing you'll wish to keep in mind: to reach 100% completion, you will need to open the corresponding save file folder, and create multiple backups (ideally, giving yourself context because it gets hard to make out the saves), because you will need to go back if you don't want to replay the game 5 or 6 times. Most of all, the save files will help you in the event that the game bugs out, as it tends to do -- for instance, when you use your keyboard to input something, and then press Enter, the game crashes; for others, some chats don't load properly; for others yet, some achievements refuse to pop up on the first or second try; and so on.


Do your due diligence to find out what's needed for 100% completion. I used Naps' guide on PlayStationTrophies.org, and made plenty of back up saves along the way. Feel free to comment if you need the files for your run, though imo it's more fun to do it along the way.

Little FMV interactive story telling game from Asian Devs, where you have to play like a Stalker / Hacker who finds a stranger's phone and has to find out what happened to the original owner.
Probably brings about 2-3 hours of semi-original fun for the main story line and one ending (of four), well worth it for the cheap price (if it's on sale) - I for instance bought Simulacra 1+2 for only 1.2€ and am already happy getting my money's worth after playing only the first part, gonna play the second one too, but beware the most expensive and newest third part is supposedly crappy according to reviews, so not gonna bother with that one.

A few Pros and Cons:

Pros:
+ neat little game, cheap price, semi-original story and idea

+ multiple Endings, somewhat of replayability (though not much)

+ some interesting charachters, an unknown protagonist, possible similarities to real live 
   dating crimes (educational)

+ some interesting Achievements in and outside of the main story line

+ nice positive review link @ the end if you liked the game & none if you click on didn't like it^^

+ very good price (at least while on sale or from external site) for Part 1&2 (not 3 though)

Cons:
- there are some small Bugs, like Soundclip getting stuck repeating in endless loop,
  or starting a vlog video while simultaneously getting a call freezes screen sideways so it gets 
  stuck and you have to restart from last checkpoint

- quite a few (very) missable Achievements, have to play at least 4 times to get them all
  (though with continue/new game+ text speed is much faster, so won't take that long)

- not many options / settings, like missing mute sound etc.

- sometimes the English wording is off (missing words, wrong grammar, etc.),
  not sure if due to Asian Dev or simulating the real chatting experience

- quite linear, except for the 4 different endings and a few choices, choices in general don't matter much,
  mostly you get like 3 Dialog options for chats etc., but in most cases it will all result in the same, maybe one 
  added sentence or a word or two changed and stuff like that


All in all I do recommend it to anyone who likes FMV / interactive and/or invesitgative / mystery Genre games.

P.S. Ashley is hot, sorry I sound like the Taylor Perv now, who is also a interesting charachter <3

review_text_raw:
Not the worst but I am surprised at how highly rated this was.
I didn't find it overly scary beyond a few jump scares.  The most believable characters in the game are Anna and her friend, I enjoyed their realistic sideconversations more than most others in this game.  The other 2 main characters were overhammed to the point of ridiculousness which was very jarring altogether.
The game gears and mechanisms running under the phone UI were just a little bit too visible to be believable.  As I found certain conversations softlocked at random points until you hit some other arbitrary checkpoint which unlocked the rest of the thread.  Also some things were just not implemented well.  In what world is a job interview carried out over text?  And every phone call was completely one-sided which was so strange - I don't know why they didn't let you select responses like in the written conversations.
Speaking of dialogue, I didn't feel I had great freedom of choice in responding in conversations - I felt I was always fighting with what I was allowed to say.  And the ending fell rather flat, with a certain character taking a complete 180 degree change in attitude and outlook just so the ending could be tied off in a semi-neat bow.
I do have the second game in the series as I got it in a bundle, and the game wasn't so awful as to put me off trying it, so I will see if these devs have taken on board lessons learned and improved things in the second go round, but this game as it stands I would not recommend it.

review_text_raw:
For full transparency: I got this game in a Humble bundle worth 0.99 cents along with 1 other game.

[b][u]The good[/u][/b]
This game has an engaging story, I was seriously invested in the characters and how this was gonna play out. The characters really had a personality to them. The performance of the person playing Anna in particular was great! 
I liked the piecing together aspect this game had and how you slowly uncover more. It managed to hold my attention, for sure. It took me on a ride that I really enjoyed.
You can see that there was a lot of time and effort put into this game, with all the different things that are on the phone and all the conversations that play out. The little image and word puzzles were a nice touch, too. The game looks good and for the most part sounds good, too. 


[b][u]The bad[/u][/b]
The big reveal at the end of the game was… meh. The mystery to the game was much more fun than the answer to that mystery. Although I did like the endings themselves and their ambiguity.  
There were some repeated grammar mistakes that took me out of the experience. Yes, it’s texting, but I feel like in texting you get more typos and less grammar mistakes. The game would benefit from fixing some of these.
The voice acting was a bit spotty. Some actors did a good job, like the detective or Taylor. However, there was one audio clip of Ashley that felt immersion-breaking to me, and Greg in general didn’t sound good to me at all, it was way over the top.

[b]I encountered a game-breaking bug.[/b] For some reason, if you go in the web browser and go to the history section, all web pages that you should only be supposed to look at later in the game are already available. If you read these, events will trigger and the game will think you’re already at those points. The game then runs both the conversations you were already having and the “new” conversations which completely breaks your savefile. So, until this bug is fixed, [b]don’t look at anything in the history section of the web browser[/b].

[b]TL;DR Nice game, I definitely recommend it! But beware of the bug I talked about ^[/b]

It's a nice experiment, based on a nice idea. But there were too many bugs -- repeated dialogues and event-chains, events triggered out-of-place -- to enjoy the game. And even disregarding the bugs, my action and dialogue choices were limited and made no sense (to me) most of the time. It's not only that suspension-of-disbelief needs to be pushed to the max to bear with it, but also that the main character (that I played) is incoherent, so it was hard to feel any connection with it.

So I spent much of my time in the game doing annoying things (repeating buggy recurring event-chains, and/or choosing actions that felt wrong) just to push the game forward.

I have never played this kind of simulation game before. I also liked this game because I like escape games. There are multiple endings. I can say that it is not very difficult and it is a short game. The game drags you towards an end according to your choices. I don't think the level of fear is too much. There are a few small jumpscares. Maybe it would be better if you turn the volume all the way up. But still not enough for a horror game. But I recommend this game because I like this kind of escape games and it is not boring. You wonder what will happen after the moves you make, and you wonder how you will reach the other endings and what will happen. Also, this is one of the reasons I recommend the game. And finally, I can say that I like the story.

review_text_raw:
Well for a "Phone Simulator" it aint a bad game. Actually I enjoyed the story a lot but there were also a couple things I didnt like.

[spoiler]The first and only timed event is a bit harsh...theres a lot of talking that you needa read before you can actually react. When you finally have control over what happens they ask you to input things that you are not familiar with at this point of the story. Yes you can know them but youre not that far into it at this point to "know" them to enter those words within 30 seconds.
Another point I didnt like is that sometimes your choice really isnt clear enough. I knew exactly what I would do in specific situations and Im presented with choices that I cant really make sense of. Sometimes the outcome went into a different direction than I intended.
Last points are about the ending. Of course I got an ending I didnt like. I saved one and sacrificed another. Im not clear as to what the entity was referring with if things went differently I could have changed its mind and Im not playing through  this again to find out. Also during the last conversations I unlocked a vlog entry and got a couple chat messages...I was unable to actually read or view them since the final conversation...well youre locked in it.[/spoiler]

Technically I had three problems with it. First when I started it I got a black screen. Im running Win10 and had to run it in Win7 compatibility mode with fullscreen optimizations disabled. Than I had no sound because for some reason it automatically switched to my turned off headset. After fixing that I could play the whole game without problems. After the credits it went to black screen again so i hadt to alt+f4 it.

Anyway...story is great if you like to read...if you like adventures with not too hard riddles...go for it...the price is cheap for the hours of entertainment that you get.

It's good but you need to be able to look past 4 big faults to really get into it, as the game can kinda work on moon logic sometimes and it sets you up for failure, not to mention a few other plot holes. 

Also the story is completely railroaded, it has multiple endings but no matter which ending you're going to get, the story and game is pretty much the exact same aside from VERY MINOR character dialog and Ashley not talking to you depending on your choices, until the final scene where it will use choices you made in the past and whether or not you do a specific thing right before the final scene, to determine if Anna and Taylor, the two main characters, are destined to die, or if not, whether or not only one of them will live or if both of them are going to live.

It only branches out and stops being railroaded in the climax and resolution of the game, and since it outright encourages you to replay it to get all the endings, it can't really get away with assuming that people will only play it once, especially since it's extremely easy to fall into the worst ending if you don't do everything right.

Outside of these things, and if you can get past it, this game is good and fun, an intriguing concept and I like Taylor even if he's a total dork. But don't play the phone version as the loops in audio are not as smooth as on the PC version and I experienced a bug that ruined every FMV in the final scene, so you should get it on steam for PC like here.

Okay, so I'm a massive fan of "Sara Is Missing" which is no longer on Steam (presumably for the extreme content) which was one of the first games Kaigan Games released based on this series, I was excited to play this as I didn't realise this game was made from the same developers, I was extremely impressed! The content isn't as extreme as SIM because I think just about anyone can say that it was extremely dark and disturbing, but I think they were trialling how a game like SIM would do, and it was successful!

Enough about SIM, Simulacra is a fantastic game! The jumpscares are timed amazingly, allowing the player to calm before the next one when they least expect it. Unlike some other games when they over exaggerate the scariness. [spoiler] (I won't lie, I jumped massively at the phone reset and Taylor's jumpscare. That was cruel haha) [/spoiler] The characters are comical, [spoiler] Especially Greg with his voice notes LMFAO[/spoiler] They all have their own individual wittiness about them, personalities and not at any point did I feel like they were lack luster, they all contributed their own to the story which I really appreciate as I find a lot of horror games tend to make characters to make the player build up a connection only them to kill them in the middle or nearer towards the end.

The only critique I'd say would be the crashing, don't get me wrong! It happens to a lot of games, but I think more frequent saving should be happening or let the player save their progress manually in case it does happen. It doesn't happen often, but on the odd occasion I've needed to restart the game. Other than that, if you like a scare, thrill and a mystery; This game is for you. Plus, it's super cheap! Try it out!

This was a surprisingly good story with a lot of content, I was expecting an hour or two of gameplay but 12 hours later here we are (100% acheivments, which are easy to get).

The acting is nothing special and the plot is never realistic in these types of games but it flow of the story and keep me interested all the way to the end.

I had no major game breaking bugs and everything worked for me even on Proton (linux).

A solid recommendation, it could do with less jump scares and more suspense.
